Two expedition carriers washing in a wide, shallow stretch of the Akobo river near Nyighum village. Evans-Pritchard notes that the expedition made its way down the Akobo towards his base at Pochala during March 1935.

A woman with a gourd vessel on her head and two men, one an elder and the other with a hunting rifle over his shoulder, photographed during the expedition's march along the Akobo river to Pochala. This village was the clan centre of the important Jowatcuaa clan (named after it's lineage founder, Ocala) although it had no headman but prominent clan elders.
A woman in Pochala village sweeping clean her compound floor with a stiff grass brush. Behind her is a thatched hut with low eaves and a grass fence.
A homestead with a granary to the left and other huts seen from a distance in open country. Several trees and garden crops can be seen growing around the homestead.

A small domed hut with a low entrance and a short section of fence behind, identified as a dry-season camp (location unknown). For villages situated at the edge of the wet season flood extent such as the districts of Ciro, Oyuaa, and Adongo along the Oboth, and Nyikaani district of the Akobo, it was often necessarily to move in the drought to locations closer to the river for fishing and everyday water needs. Since Evans-Pritchard was in Anuakland during the drought he was able to photograph shelters used during this time of the year.

A man wearing a long textile body cloth, walking through long grass, identified as a nobleman of Digiira village, an area under the influence of the Nyigoc lineage. Evans-Pritchard identifies one of two nobles living in this village, namely Agaanya-war-Uliimi.

A group of carriers in the distance during a march across Anuakland savannah towards Pocama, presumably heading towards Akobo. This sort of sparsely wooded plain is characteristic of western Anuakland in Adongo district, and may have been taken during his march back to Akobo in May 1935.

This is a view of Mount Homa taken from Kendu Bay. Both the mountain and the lake shore township of Kendu Bay are in Karachuonyo Location of South Nyanza. The mountain is a major volcanic plug in the Lake Victoria Basin and is only a couple of kilometres from the lake. From the higher hills above Kendu Bay the land drops quickly into a low plain area and this leaves the mountain to stand out spectacularly. Mt. Home is associated with some hot springs, carbonate soda (bala) for medicine and cooking, and a number of Luo beliefs about their ancestors. In particular, there is a traditional belief about a big snake, known as Nyangoe, who is supposed to live there and who could cause hurricanes if not appeased. [Gilbert Oteyo 9/9/2004]

The house of one of the daughters of Koi Kadisa, a Yeyi woman living in Sanyedi ward. The daughter had grown older and wanted her own house on the plot. Since she was working at one of the safari lodges (Maun Lodge) she wanted to use the same letlhaka (water reeds, Phragmites australis) that they regularly use for buildings since she liked it. She adapted the style of the house from one of the safari lodge buildings she stayed in at Maun Lodge.

He used to have a lot of cattle but after lung disease he used the compensation payments to build. The other side of him is the house and lolwapa of his wife's mother who has come to live with them, and the round mud brick hut to the right belongs to his son. The plot in general is especially well kept and maintained, with renewed letlhaka courtyard fencing that many found increasingly expensive to buy.

A view down from the side of a steep hill, possibly Belinian, towards a Bari homestead, comprising a large and several smaller huts in a fenced compound. The Seligmans carried out investigations among the Bari of Belinian and Ali Bey in Jan 1922, before moving south to the Torit area among the Lotuko-speaking people there.

An upper body profile portrait of a Bari girl sitting with hands together. She is wearing strings of beads around the neck and numerous short horizontal lines of cicatrices on her upper arm. It seems likely that this image was taken shortly before October 1878 when Buchta reached Lado (Juba) on board S.S. Safia.

An old grind stone containing pieces of quartz and with old cooking stones nearby, marking the grave of the Belinian rain-maker's father. Next to the grave is an ebony post (feiti) which was notched near the top, a common feature of Bari graves. It is noted that the sacrifice for rain was undoubtedly carried out at this grave-shrine, when the rain stones held by the rain-maker were brought here to be anointed as part of a ceremony. The Seligmans carried out investigations among the Bari of Belinian and Ali Bey in Jan 1922, before moving south to the Torit area among the Lotuko-speaking people there.

A group portrait of two Bari (Fajelu) men with a woman between them in front of a hut. The man to the left has a quiver over his shoulder, bow and spears at his feet (one a large hunting spear). The man to the right has white feather hair decoration. The woman is wearing strings of beads around her neck. Buchta made an excursion to the groups west of the Nile in 1879 setting out from Juba on 7th July and returning there on 26th August.

At the bottom on the back there is a horizontal section of woven blue, red, white, and tan lozenge shapes; tassels in blue, white, red, and brown along the bottom edge at the back.

Circular openwork rigid basket with handle. The base is made of parallel whole canes lashed with split cane to a single cross-piece and nailed to a cane ring foot. The sides consist of two bands of continuous interlocking figures of eight in centre cane, separated by a rigid band of whole cane wrapped in split cane. The border is also of whole cane wrapped in split cane. The handle consists of three whole canes wrapped in split cane: the three canes divide above the basket, the centre one being nailed to the base and the outer two curving round to be incorporated in the border.

A view of the rocky hill settlement of Logurun, visited by the Seligmans in the early part of 1922. According to their diary they travelled between these villages by bicycle. Logurun contained an important Lotuko rain shrine, and was part of the Tarangole territorial group within the Lotuko-speaking peoples. The homesteads were built on terraces irregularly up the hillside.
Lotuko blacksmiths working a bellows under a tree.

Two women, one seemingly breast-feeding a toddler, sit underneath a shelter or granary on a mat, with some crops, probably ground-nuts, on the floor nearby. The woman in the foreground has her hair shaved at the sides to leave a central section. In the section of cultivation seen beyond are stalks of ripening millet. Since groundnuts and some millet were harvested in August and September, this suggests that these women are taking a break from harvesting activity probably during the hottest part of the day.

A three-quarter length portrait of a woman wearing a waist cloth and holding a pipe in her mouth, standing amongst tall maize plants. Around her neck are a variety of bead and metal chain ornaments. In another image she is described simply as an unmarried girl.

A group of Mandari children. A girl is wearing a waist string with a fringe of ?leather pieces hanging down from metal links and is holding a gourd on her head. In front of her is a small boy with distended stomach carrying a baby on his back in a sling. An older boy, also with a distended stomach, sits on a rock above them watching. It is likely that these children are quite malnourished judging from their stomach distension.

An upper body portrait of two Mandari girls wearing waist-cloths and strings of beads around their necks, one leaning against the thatch of a hut. Beads worn by girls around the neck were often given by male admirers. They both have forehead scarification after the manner of the Dinka, and the girl in the foreground has a series of linear scar marks on her abdomen, although for the Mandari it does not denote any formal initiation (hence her use of it along with the youths), and was used instead for aesthetically pleasing effect.

A head-and-shoulders group portrait of a Mandari youth resting his hands on the shoulders of a girl either side of him. The girls are wearing strings of neck beads, probably gifted to them by their male admirers, and the girl in the foreground has forehead scar patterns in the manner of the Dinka, although for the Mandari this did not constitute part of an initiation process.

A portrait of a kneeling Mandari mother holding her baby in her left arm, a goat standing near her right arm. She is wearing a married woman's goat-skin apron as well as a neck string of what may be teeth.

A full length portrait of a Mandari woman with two girls, one carrying a baby and a gourd water container in a carrying net. The other girl is carrying a large basketry covered container on her head. They are all wearing colourful beads in a variety of colours around their necks and waists. Such bead strings were often given to young women by courting male youths.
A three-quarter length portrait of a Mandari man wearing several strings of waist beads standing with two young women in a homestead, the step thatch of a hut visible behind them [poor photo].
An upper body full face portrait of a Mandari youth wearing a textile head-wrap and plume, with string of flat-face beads around the base.

An upper body full face portrait of a Mandari youth, wearing a number of strings of rem waist beads. The colour configuration of these beads exhibited relative age-grade status. Age-grades among the western Mandari seem to have been a relatively recent, loosely defined or organized borrowing by youths from their Atuot neighbours, there being no memory of age-grades or even initiation in the past.

A group of young Mandari men seated on the ground, several of whom are holding spears. On their heads some are wearing textile head wraps. Just beyond them a woman with a small child are also sitting on the ground.
A three-quarter length portrait of a man in the uniform of the Anglo-Egyptian Condominium authority (1899-1955) holding a rifle over his shoulder and wearing an ammunition belt and hat with plume.

A portrait of Jean Buxton with camera, sitting on the verandah of a brick building of the colonial administration, probably in Tali. Next to her is the Mandari sergeant, Makelele Nyayo, who was charged with looking after her personal safety.
Decorative element from a girl's apron, made of square ostrich eggshell and brown spherical beads laced together with a strip of hide.

A formal group portrait of young Luo men dressed as warriors with headdresses and other ornaments, some holding clubs. They are described as belonging to the Nyakach clan, which also lends its name to an administrative location. Those standing have head gears made of vegetation and animal fur. One of them (3rd right standing) has head gear of Colobus monkey tail sewn with cowrie shells. They are also adorned with armlets and and leg rings of metal (minyonge) and hide, bead necklaces (tikng’ut) and cowrie shell belts (okanda gaagi) across the chest and waist. Cartons of sorghum beer (Chibuku brand) stacked together and used as firewood. The typical way of burning logs was end-on in this manner, pushing them gradually further inwards as they burned down. Since the population of Maun had increased, firewood was impossible to find close to the town centre, and people would need to go further and further afield to collect it. This meant that some people has to burn waste in this way to survive.

Over-exposed close-up image of decoratively carved grave marker by a roadside. It has KHARALA carved on the top (see image 2008.78.2.40). This is one of a number of old wooden grave markers along the road from Mundri to Amadi.  A village can be seen behind. The road-builders moved the road specially to avoid the grave markers. Informant Andrea told us that these grave markers were used before the current style of  graves as seen in informant Deborah's compound (see 2008.78.1.38). Deborah's account of them was that grave markers were used when there was no body, if the family member had died far away - to bring the 'soul' home. This grave marker has three 'rings' carved at the top. There used to be specialist craftsmen who made the grave markers. Patti Langton [26/05/2009]

A stone mound erected over a man's grave (dodo) surmounted by a short pointed stake with a decorated gourd attached to it. Around the mound are six carved posts tallying different large animals killed by the deceased, one of which (to the right) is also surmounted by a carved likeness of the man. These carved figures were considered representations of the deceased, put up to honour the individual, but not serving any ritual purpose [cloudy image].

A rain-making shrine of an unusual type compared to other Bongo rain-posts (riyak), and rather more like in form a Zande tuka or ancestral shrine. It was situated under a large tree, with ground swept well around it. The female operator of the shrine threw water over it with an invocation to spirits during drought, since she was widely considered to be possessed and closely associated with ancestral spirits. Directly behind it is a grave mound with forked tally grave post.

A set of old stone axe-heads and other stone tools, laid out on the ground by Surur the rain-maker for Evans-Pritchard to photograph them (although not touch them) from their home along with his hair clippings in a pot beneath the eaves of his stake-walled hut. These stones were called landa loma - stones of Loma, a spiritual connection with rain-making. During rain-making Surur would place these stones along with magical medicines in a pot with rock-pool water and sprinkle to the east where the next day was to arrive from [light leakage on negative?].

A stone mound erected over a woman's grave (dodo) with two carved posts tallying the number of large or dangerous animals killed by her husband as a means of honouring her. The post on the right has a tin basin affixed to the top, possibly for receiving offerings.

A stone mound erected over a man's grave (dodo) surmounted by a short pointed stake (visible to left) with a carved pot pierced over it. Around the mound are six carved posts tallying different large animals killed by the deceased, two of which are visible in this image, one with a likeness of the deceased carved at the top. These carvings were understood as a means of honouring the dead but did not have any particular ritual meaning.

A figure carving with a small straw hat representing a deceased man, set close to his grave mound also surmounted with hunting tallies, as a means of honouring him. Evans-Pritchard describes this figure as having bead eyes, the face being stained blue with a dye bought from an Arab merchant, and the body being painted red with red ochre.

A stone mound near a hut erected over a man's grave (dodo) with three carved posts surmounting the top tallying twenty elephants killed in the hunt by the deceased, placed as a means of honouring him. Around the mound are five more carved posts (some with arrows stuck in them). Two are visible in this image: a carved post in the likeness of the deceased (?wearing a hat) with a tally of two hippo killed, and in the foreground a forked post tallying six rhino.

A head-and-shoulders profile portrait of a man with hair ash-plastered into a forward facing 'horn', leaning against a colonial brick building at Pek. Hair was plastered in this way as part of the process of dying the hair a reddish tint. The image was taken by A. N. Tucker, who worked as Linguistic Expert of non-Arabic languages for the Sudan Government from 1929 to 1931. Evans-Pritchard met Tucker when the latter visited his fieldsite in 1930, after which time he gave him these prints.

View of a large stone carving at the ancient Maya site of Quirigua located near the banks of the Motagua river in the department of Izabal, Guatemala. The photograph shows a man standing beside the west side of a carved stone stela known by archaeologists as Stela D, as it was first described by Alfred Maudslay in his seminal publication of the Quirigua site in his multi-volume Archaeology (1889–1902): 'The Initial Series of the inscription [...] may, I think, be read as follows: [...] On the west side: (1) 9th Cycle; (2) 16th Katun; (3) 13th Ahau; (4) 4th Chuen; (5) 17th Day; (6) 8 Caban, (11, second half of glyph) 5 Yaxkin. On the east side the full count of chuens and days makes the reckoning fairly easy. On the west side the difficulty is greater'. More recent scholarship dates the stela (also known as Monument 4) to 9.16.15.0.0, 7 Ahau 18 Pop (Maya calendar), or A.D. 766 in the standard Western (Gregorian) calendar. The monument was created during the later part of the sixty-year reign of K'ak' Tiliw Chan Yopaat. It was one of a number of stelae and zoomorphs erected at Quirigua as part of a complex building programme which took place at the height of the city-state's power during the Late Classic period, and whose primary aim was to legitimate and reinforce the power of the ruler.

View of multi-storeyed buildings surrounding the main plaza of Zia pueblo, with people standing or resting in and around the square.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), the 'village is now almost in ruins.  It is constructed of small lava rocks laid in mortar, the houses sometimes reaching a height of three stor[ey]s. [...] This village, unlike its neighbour, Santa Ana, is situated on the edge of a high rocky mesa and is not liable to sand burial.'  The rocks and branch in the foreground of the photograph remain from an earlier structure which was not rebuilt.

View (looking westward) of buildings at Laguna pueblo, located on on the Rio Laguna river (a tributary of the Rio Grande), about sixty miles west of Isleta.  According to James Stevenson's original note for this photograph (prepared circa 1885), Laguna's 'earlier location was thirty miles north of the present village, but from time to time during the last three or four centuries changes have been made until the present location of the village was reached. [...] The photograph shows quite clearly the beauty and compactness of this typical pueblo.

Kamawa', or shoulder bag, made of tree anteater hide, used by men for ammunition etc. The main body of the bag is rectangular and has coarse, dark brown fur. The bag is held closed by a catch, formed from the animal's lighter brown tail, which is wrapped round the bag; a wooden peg which fits through a hole in the tail forms the fastening. A string shoulder strap is affixed to the top corners.

Wapa. A shallow, round tray made from plaited basketry with frames of cane attached by fibre to the inside and outside of the rim. Plaited brown and natural geometric pattern and a central square with four frog motifs. Loop of thin fibre attached to the frame.

Quiver and darts for use with a blow gun. Quiver made from a hollowed length of bamboo, one end stuffed with cotton or cotton palm fibre; basketry collar made from black and plain cane strips attached near the middle of the quiver and flaring towards the top. Darts present in one end, three wrapped with cotton and fibre.

Ear adornments made from metal triangles made from repurposed Pepsi Cola cans threaded onto fine strings with glass beads. Beads alternate between light blue and white, with one strand having a single red bead; both earrings have one dark blue bead. Earrings are kept together with knotted string.
Model of birch bark bailer sewn together along one side and around the base. Hide handle with knots at both ends.

Beer filter made from half of a gourd or 'tete' used to strain chewed yucca from liquid. 13 Rows of holes spiral outwards from the base.

Ginger root used for coughs and as a purgative. Eaten as it is.

Spectacle case made by Irina Nutti. Made from reindeer leather (sisti) and decorated with woollen cloth and pewter thread. The case is rounded at both ends, one end open (for insertion of spectacles) this end can be closed with vecro strips (sewn on the inside). One side and the bottom have a seams, along which has been sewn green woollen cloth. A diamond shape has been cut from the front of the case, in this has been sewn blue woollen cloth, this has been outlined with a thin strip of green woollen cloth. In the centre of the blue cloth has been sewn pewter thread in a much embellished cross shape (which has arms of equal length).

Cup - Wooden double cup depicting carved human figures, an unidentified animal and geometric designs. Cups separated by centralstru, which extends at ends, potentially used as a handle. The shape of the cups can be described as quadrangular, while the four sides are almost bent in a sickle shape. Two corners/angles of the cups are sharp and two are flattened. Condition fair: One crack on one handle, two holes on the other one.

Box - Rectangular box with lid secured by metal hinges. The lid is carved what appears to be a hunting scene, with human figures and deer-like animals in relief, which are surrounded by two double-headed snakes. Bands of triangles are carved along the four corners of the base.

Gamuts. Man’s headdress of black velvet, glass beads, pig or boar skin and tusks. Body of headdress consists of sturdy upright band wrapped in velvet, reverse secured with plaited ties in red, yellow and green synthetic wool. Lower exterior decorated with band of cowrie shells, enclosed top and bottom with bands of muted orange and green beads; small repeated triangles of dark green beads run along top band. Upper front and sides covered with pig or boar skin with coarse brown upright hair; pig or boar tail extends upright from centre front. Circular ornament at centre front of muted green and orange beads in alternating triangular pattern, encircled by eleven large tusks, with conus shell disc at centre; further small multicoloured bead at centre of conus disc.
Cloth - Piece of dark blue cloth, with embroidery in yellow, red and green. The pattern is called " Tomoan"

Necklace - Woman’s necklace. Three rows of orange; yellow/green and multi-coloured disc-shaped glass beads, with rectangular shell spacers, arranged in multiple groups of 6 or 7 beads, alternating with single beads. The central section consists of multi-coloured beads. Secured with black and white plaited threads.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Punan, a Kota man.

Mbulu ngulu. Reliquary guardian figure of wood, plated with hammered copper and brass. In the centre is a concave human face with crescent eyes and a pointed triangular nose; the face is decorated with a plain cross, the arms spanning the length and width of the face, and panels of incised diagonal lines. There is an abstract head ornament, with a rectangular panel with rounded upper corners behind the head, and a semicircular panel above the head, decorated with stamped dots around the edges and crosshatched triangles along the bottom. There are two conical protrusions along the bottom of the head ornament, one on each side. The figure has a ribbed cylindrical neck and a open lozenge-shaped piece that indicates the body.
Ma'hi'k. A necklace made by Sherbegum. It has five strands of twisted black cotton thread with elongated oval yellow plastic beads tightly threaded onto the cotton thread. Part of a Kalasha costume.
Spoon - Flat spoon, said to be made of deer horn. Reddish in colour
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Haokholet, a Kuki man from Paklang village, Ukhoul subdivision of Manipur State.
Taungi. Drum, Taungi (T-K) Paduchhyan (C-K). Hemispherical, copper body with calf or goat skin made by leather-maker.

Shairu Choh. Arrow. Bunch of porcupine quills projecting from a metal holder. Quills will fly by themselves,. They are projected forward by a Pa-chyu shaman and the quill turns and the pointed end spears a bad spirit and brings it back. Can also be used to fight with another shaman.
Spoon - Small, wooden spoon, with handle curving upwards sharply from bowl
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Lepo Bodra, a twenty-four year-old Ho woman who worked for the Tata Iron and Steel Co. plant in Jamshedpur.
Malagai. Summer hat, made of velvet and silk, dark blue with a red tassel at the top. The hat is pointed, with a turned up velvet brim.
Bös. A long rectangular dark blue silk sash with design in the weft.

Buryat Ulgii. A child's cot with teeg and fox talisman. It is made from loosely woven textile wrapped around and stitched onto a rectangular wooden frame. There are four cords of braided white fibre, possibly silk or synthetic, attached at the four corners and tied together with a loop at the top for suspension. Four padded triangles in black, green and red silk brocade, wool tassels and a fox talisman made from felted animal hair hang from the centre of the knotted cords.
Costume. Gold hair ornament in shape of waisted oval, with two pointed ends curving upwards. Engraved with linear patterns and animal heads.
Bracelet, made from a strip of copper alloy, probably brass, which has been bent into a penannular shape. The edge of the bracelet has been decorated with circular and semicircular impressions.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of paris of Kaira, a Veddah man from Danigala village, Sri Lanka.
Clay bowl of black fabric with a wide mouth, rounded base and a slightly flared lip. The bowl has been used for cooking and has charcoal remnants on the exterior.
Mallet - Wooden mallet used in the manufacture of Tibetan paper. Consists of two pieces of wood.
Cup - Beer mug made from the bamboo Dendrocalanus Hamiltonii. Lid made from joint of same bamboo. Two handles threaded through bottom of mug and fixed at top with plait-work.
Belt - Long, thin, cane belt made by Dafla women, and worn by both women and men.

Oplecko. Woman's shirt. White with embroidered decorations in red, purple, green, blue, black, orange, and white around the cuffs and the neckline. The sleeves are gathered at the puffs. There are ties at the front.

Lajblik. Woman's vest. The vest is comprised of panels of floral fabric with red flower designs and further panels of pink ?satin. The front has two lines of sequins surrounded by ?lace, and plastic buttons for fastening. The back and hem also has further lace decoration.
Square white lace table cloth. Four central flowers are surrounded by swirling patterns.
White macramé vest. There are pads of cotton balls woven into the body of it, and rope-like tassels at the bottom.

Narwhal or whale ivory model of Nenets village with trees, a chum tent, reindeer, human figures, etc. mounted on a rectangular platform. Depicts scenes from life of harnessing reindeer, childbirth and a bear hunt. Inaccuracies in the harness, ceremonies involving acts of kneeling and raised hands draw on stereotypical views of Nenets' culture and was created by a non-Indigenous carver, possibly as part of the Tobol'sk workshops

A doll made from a strip of felt with strips of yellow, purple, blue, and red fabric sewn to the back. Two strips of blue fabric are sewn to the front at the top, with bead decorations. The head of the doll is made of the top half of a bird's beak with part of the skin of the bird's head attached to the fur.

Tamata. Votive offering. Stylised representation of a face and neck, modelled in wax. Reverse flat. It is mainly olive green in colour with some patches of black, the eyes are represented by black-eyed beans. A loop of string protrudes from the top of its head, suggesting a point of suspension.
Tamata. Votive offering. Representation of a heart, modelled in green wax. A string loop protrudes from the wide end suggesting a point of suspension.

Hanging religious charm with colour printed pictures on both sides; Madonna & Child and St. Christopher. Each picture is surrounded by a row of sequins secured by small beads and metal pins. The edge of the central disc has radiating, cylindrical beads tipped with small, round beads and sequins. At the top and bottom of the central disc are rosettes of circular, flat beads and there are large, round beads on the outer edges. Attached to the top is a gold coloured metal chain for suspension. A gold coloured, plastic cross hangs from the bottom, flanked by two translucent plastic strawberries.

Tamata. Votive offering. Stylistic representation of an ear, stamped on thin, silver sheeting to produce a slightly raised design. The ear has an elongated shape and a spiral design in the centre. Detail incised around the outline. There is a semicircular tab and hole at the top for the attachment of a pin.

Sää’mvaacc in Skolt Sami. Pair of large mittens, made by Matleena Fofanoff, from hand carded, hand-spun, and knitted wool. The main body of the mittens is made of cream, non-dyed wool. Around the wrist area is a blue and red pattern of lozenges, bordered by blue, red and yellow stripes. The mittens are tied together at the top with red, blue, yellow, and cream plaited wool. Original tag is attached.

Water drum. Slightly waisted tubular drum with solid figure carved on front that has flat face rear. Penis intact, its tip covered with green gloss paint. Eye inlay lost and sockets painted with green gloss. Rougher face design than 1935.23B. At back lug formed by pierced neck extension which is near base of head. Two thicknesses of rough cane tied through this lug.

Bag netted from thick twine in double figure of 8 rows. Design in contrasting reddish brown and dull blue netted in against natural pale brown colour. Made by Tshuosh, in neighbourhood of Berui village. Carried suspended from the head by women.

Carved fowl's head, broken off at neck, touches of red and white paint on crest. Narrow raised beak and cheek to eye design. Slight piercing of cheek pouches. Figure broken. Original accession notes: " Carving of a domestic fowl, ? part of a lime pot." Fair
Lime box. Bamboo tube with wooden ornament in shape of a janus-face at top of barred ovoid, with a bird on a 'nose' at the ovoid's tip. Decorated with blue. white and red paint and many tassels.

Flattish profile fret carving, with relief design of one main human face, and four others, two of which are double faces. Nassa shell inlay in the eyes of the main face, which has a pierced nose and pierced ears with tassel through them and through the chin.

Ovoid wooden head with small cap top, curved back. Yellow with a little red colouring. Thick-lipped oval mouth. Narrow slanting eyes, joined to cap. Pierced delicate club shape nose. Chin extension, unpierced arch to chin tip.
Lens-shaped wooden head with raised eyebrow curves, oval ring and dot eyes, flattened club nose. Covered in red pigment. Attached to 1930.278 with native string.

Necklace of plaited string work in form of face with 5 medium length tails on lower edges, 2 ear loops and stub in centre of top edge. Bulbous forehead with cowrie shell eyes below. Ribbed nose loop with no ornaments. Rear of face has loop in centre with 4 rough lengths twined string attached. Broad neck band which fastens by loop on one end and large knot on the other. Whole covered with black and faint remains of red pigment.

Arrow with wooden point with small widely spaced alternate side barbs. No foreshaft. Shaft binding of roughly coiled very fine cane or tough fibre (?). Tapering bamboo shaft with remains of red stain.
Bracelet made of two parallel strings of cylindrical coconut beads which are connected by carved letters strung between them. The letters spell the personal name "LUCIANA".
A necklace made of spherical brown seeds with vertical ridges. Some of the seeds have small holes on the surface.
Dinki. Pair of leather boots, topped with white cloth. Band of black cloth around the top, decorated with embroidered motifs in cream, yellow, pink, orange, red, and green.

A round black silk cap, made of six triangles sewn together and with panels of patterned gold and black silk in between; the bottom is trimmed the same patterned gold and black silk, stitched into pleats. Embroidered curvilinear design on the front. Interior lined with red cloth; symbol in black ink printed on inside.
Pair of child's brown leather soled shoes with beige uppers. The sole material is gathered around the toes.

Female genital covering made of leaves with a circular basketry projection at tone end. The basketry is woven in two-tone to give a checkerboard pattern. Leaves are layered over the covering and stitched along the outside edge.

Pot with lid, both of burnished black ware. Lid [.1] hemispherical in shape with centred, rounded handle. Decorated with pattern above base. Pot [.2] with inverted rim, rounded body and flat base. Decorated with horizontal band of chevrons.

Pot of burnished red ware. Everted rim, short neck, shouldered body and flat base. Decorated below shoulder with linear patterns incised with a stick. Four horizontal bands surrounding three rows of filled triangles. Horizontal band above base.
Small burnished pot with straight sides and a wide rim with a short spout. The pot is decorated with incised horizontal lines below the rim and above the base.

Globular pot of orange clay with a flat base, pronounced neck with an everted rim and glazed interior. Below the neck is a band of horizontal notches. The base has blackened areas. There is evidence of historic pest and damage.
Pot of burnished red ware. Inverted rim, rounded body and flat base. Decorated with triangular patterns. Black firing marks on base. Section missing from rim.

Leather quiver filled with arrows. The arrows have sagittal-shaped socketed iron heads with three or more barbs on each side: shafts slender about 540mm in length without notches, and some with leaf-feathering. The quiver is made of leather and is a flat rectangle, stitched into shape. A handle made of plaited plant fibre attached to the quiver.

Zither, comprising shallow wooden trough with slots at each end for eight strings. Two cross-shaped and one slot-shaped perforation in the bottom. Geometric decoration on back and rim, incised and blackened. Loop of twisted plant fibre cord threaded through two holes on one side. Some strings are preserved, secured by wooden toggles.

A wooden headrest. The upper section has an upward curving oblong shape. The middle section has a narrow cross-section and is roughly rectangular in shape, each side is decorated with carved linear markings. There is a loop of hide tied through two holes. On a hemispherical base. Carved in relief from a single piece of light coloured wood.

A long rectangular piece of cream cotton. It is embroidered with geometric patterns in grey along the two long edges; it is woven with pink and grey stripes towards one short edge, with geometric embroidery in grey in between the stripes.

Female's funerary ornament, cuboid in shape, inner part covered in white cotton sewn with blue thread, this is then wrapped with blue wool string in a pattern forming concentric squares on bottom and top faces, reddish pink twine is wrapped above the blue forming squares with a cross on side faces. At the centre of the top face is a round flat disc embellished with strings of beads in silver and blue, probably glass, on each corner of the cube is a flat disc with the same glass or plastic blue and silver beads, and from the base, two more beaded discs hang from reddish pink thread, discs are sewn on with green thread.
A necklace consisting of small faceted gold gilt beads strung onto a length of plant fibre. It is fastened with a copper alloy spring ring clasp.

Necklace with pointed ovoid pendants, made from brass with possible gilding. 15 pendants with a horizontal pointed ovoid form hanging from a faceted ring; pendants alternate with groups of seven or eight faceted beads; fastened with a loop of cotton cord and one of the pendants. Strung on white cotton cord.
Bead necklace. Worn by men and women.
End-blown cane flute with three stops and incised ornamentation.

Man's black cotton loin cloth (1949.747 A), rectangular in shape, three thin double lines of white, short edges finished in red with two thing stripes of double white lines. One long edge with exposed warp, possibly to allow rope for tying (1949.747 B) to pass through.
Portrait sculpture in plaster of Eravalu Lingaru, a sixteen year-old man from the Chenchu community in Pulajelma.

Large hide shield. The front has two vertical lines of hide stitching and is decorated with faded patterns in white, black and red. There is a boss in the centre. Wooden handle at the back with coiled leather straps connecting the top and the bottom to the handle, and a leather strap linking the handle to one of the sides. Circular handguard of leather, notched on the outside.

Rotuet ap chok. Sword with leather sheath. The sword has a wooden handle and metal blade; blade has a midrib and flares towards the terminal. The sheath has a midrib and is stitched down the centre of one side. The other side has an arched handle, through which a leather belt is threaded.
Simple bow with plant fibre string. Wooden bow with circular cross-section tapering towards either end; iron spiral around tip of bow at top; band of hide to prevent string slipping at top.

Korket. A hearth. Carved wooden stick of sub-cylindrical shape, one end has three holes, the other tapers to a point. The three holes are partially broken and show evidence of fire damage; caused by the friction of a drill. Poinik (fire-stick) consists of a korket (hearth) used with a kirkit (drill) to start a fire by hand through surface friction.

Pair of woman’s shoe of the pattern known as Kalati. Turned up toes embroidered with metal and coloured thread and decorated with green and gold leather; patches of different coloured, embroidered cloth on insole; low shoe with red edges; leather soles.

Walking stick, comprising a thick, cylindrical, segmented shaft, possibly of palm wood, with a metal band covering each end. A black tassel, possibly of wool with a fibre binding and ribbon, is tied through metal-lined oval holes near the top of the shaft. The metal band at the bottom is wide; the band at the top is narrow.

A short jacket made from black wool, with a brown cotton braided trim. The jacket has long sleeves that are open along the bottom and connected at the cuffs with the brown trim. Internal pockets on both sides.
Lapudzi. Pair of woollen socks knitted with a ribbed cuff in stripes of blue, pink and orange.

A waistcoat with an open front fastened with four toggles of black cord at the bottom and one at the neck. Made from blue cotton cloth striped with yellow vertical lines, with red and purple velvet panels down the front, overlaid with decorative black braiding. The arm holes and the bottom are trimmed with black cotton; the inside is lined with white cotton across the body and black and blue floral silk along the edges.
A pair black garters woven into long rectangular bands with loops and one end, and long plaited ties with tassels ends at the other.

Beaded ornament in the form of a snake, comprising a long, red textile tube decorated with coloured glass beads, with a lozenge-shaped head and loops of pink, blue, black and white beads for the tail. The head is green with white eyes, and has pink, blue and colourless chevrons on the underside. The body has blue-green, beige, blue, colourless, red, and pink circles on a green background on one side, and yellow on the underside.

A folding pocket knife with a black handle made of horn, carved in the form of a dragon. Red pigment has been used to highlight the dragon's mouth and eyes. The blade is metal and has a curved cutting edge and a point along the blade back. There is a star engraved on one side of the blade, and a fish and "BAEINIKI" [sic] on the other. There is a suspension ring attached to the end of the blade.
A wooden tool used to straighten spears. Formed from a roughly cylindrical stick, one end is wider and has an oval cut out.
Square iron cowbell and clapper, with a plaited looped leather strap. The bell is damaged.

Armlet made of plaited hide. Attached is a bundle of hairs from a giraffe's tail some of the hairs havee been twisted or plaited. The bundle is bound at the top with lizard skin and a length of twisted string.
A cover for containers; rectangular in shape. Made from reeds bound together at each end with plaited plant fibre.
Twin-bowled pipe. The two bowls are of black clay, globular in shape, with a band of delicate incised decoration below the rim. The stem, made of wood or cane, has split.

Drum with cylindrical wooden body and a truncated conical base. The head has an ox hide skin for playing, and the lower part is also encased in ox hide. Straight lacing down the length of the drum, made of thin twisted strips of leather, affix the two pieces of ox hide to each other and hold them in place. There are two hide loops around the head, connected with a hide strap.
